hints: Look past where the pathogens are found and focus on what HIV actually does to the body, especially to helper T-lymphocytes and immunity.
Remember that AIDS is an immunodeficiency, so think about how a weakened immune system would handle a second pathogen like Plasmodium.
walkthrough:
**Recall what HIV/AIDS does**

Think like a biologist first. HIV infects and destroys helper T-lymphocytes. Without enough of these, the whole specific immune response becomes very weak.

This is why AIDS is called an acquired immunodeficiency.

**Link this to malaria**

The malaria pathogen, Plasmodium, still enters the body in the normal way, by mosquito bite. A healthy immune system can often control it to some extent.

In a person with HIV/AIDS, that control is lost because antibody production, T-cell activation and phagocyte coordination all depend on helper T-cells.

**Choose the immune explanation**

So the higher occurrence is not because the two diseases travel together or help each other directly. It is because immunosuppression leaves the person vulnerable to infection and to more severe disease.

options.A: Many pathogens travel in blood, but simply being in the blood does not make malaria more common in HIV patients.
options.B: Malaria is transmitted by mosquito bite, not by blood-to-blood transmission like HIV, so shared transmission does not explain the link.
options.C: HIV does infect T-lymphocytes, but Plasmodium infects liver cells and red blood cells, it does not use T-lymphocytes.
options.D: Correct. HIV destroys helper T-cells and suppresses immunity, so the immune response to Plasmodium is weaker and malaria occurs more often and more severely.
